questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
questions.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: A checked exception is an `Exception` subtype other than `RuntimeException`; Java requires callers to catch it or declare it. `RuntimeException` and `Error` subtypes are unchecked. Checked status is a compile-time API rule, not proof that a failure is recoverable, and unchecked exceptions are not limited to programming bugs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can define the compiler-enforced distinction and place exceptions correctly under RuntimeException or not
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Equating checked with recoverable and unchecked with programming bug instead of describing the catch-or-declare rule
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the exact hierarchy boundary and explain that recoverability belongs to the caller's context

sections.title: The Line Is Drawn at RuntimeException
sections.content:
The difference is a **compile-time rule**. A checked exception is an `Exception` subtype that is not a `RuntimeException`; code that can let it escape must catch it or declare it with `throws`. `RuntimeException` subclasses and all `Error` subclasses are unchecked, so Java does not require catch-or-declare.

That hierarchy does not decide whether a failure is recoverable. `IOException` may be recoverable or fatal for the current operation. An unchecked exception may represent a programming defect, invalid caller input, a missing database row, or another condition chosen by an API. The API designer selects the category and callers still decide what they can handle.

Both kinds are thrown at runtime. 'Checked' means checked by the compiler, not detected earlier or safer.

sections.title: Checked vs Unchecked
sections.content:
| Aspect | Checked | Unchecked |
|---|---|---|
| Parent | `Exception` (not `RuntimeException`) | `RuntimeException` |
| Compiler enforcement | Must `catch` or declare `throws` | None |
| Models | Recoverable external failure | Programming bug / misuse |
| Examples | `IOException`, `SQLException` | `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException` |
| Typical response | Handle / retry | Fix the code |

sections.title: Two Categories at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Checked|~Compile-time rule|Exception outside RuntimeException|catch or declare when it escapes|recovery depends on caller
emerald|Unchecked|~No catch-or-declare|RuntimeException and Error|may still be documented and handled|severity is separate
amber|Boundary|~Hierarchy decides category|RuntimeException branch is unchecked|other Exception types are checked|Error is unchecked
rose|Name trap|~Not about timing|both kinds are thrown at runtime|checked means compiler-checked|not a recovery label

sections.title: Checked: compiler forces you to handle it
Unchecked needs nothing; checked needs catch or throws
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating the difference as timing** — every exception is thrown at runtime; `checked` only means the compiler checks it at compile time.
- **Assuming unchecked is less serious** — a `NullPointerException` can take down an app just as hard as any checked failure.
- **Forgetting `Error` is unchecked too** — `OutOfMemoryError` and friends sit outside the checked rule alongside `RuntimeException`.
- **Wrapping every call in `try`/`catch` to quiet the compiler** — only checked exceptions need handling; blanket-catching `RuntimeException` hides real bugs.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Checked:** `Exception` subtype outside the `RuntimeException` branch.
- **Catch or declare:** required when a checked exception can escape.
- **Unchecked:** `RuntimeException` and `Error` branches.
- **Not a recovery label:** either category can be recoverable or fatal for a particular operation.
- **API decision:** choose a meaningful type and document what callers can do.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Checked and unchecked describe Java's compile-time handling rule. A checked exception is an `Exception` subclass that is not a `RuntimeException`, so code must catch it or declare it when it can escape. `RuntimeException` subclasses and `Error` subclasses are unchecked.

For example, `Files.readString(path)` can throw the checked `IOException`, so a method either handles that failure or declares `throws IOException`. Calling `Integer.parseInt("abc")` can throw the unchecked `NumberFormatException`; Java does not force a catch or declaration. That does not mean every checked failure is recoverable or every unchecked failure is a programmer bug. Recovery depends on the caller and the application boundary. The category mainly tells callers what the type system requires and forms part of the API contract.

questions.question: Can you give examples of commonly used checked exceptions in Java?
questions.title: Common Checked Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: The most common checked exceptions are **`IOException`** (and subtypes like `FileNotFoundException`), **`SQLException`** (JDBC), **`InterruptedException`** (thread interruption), **`ClassNotFoundException`** (reflection/class loading), and **`ParseException`**. They all extend `Exception` (not `RuntimeException`), so the compiler forces you to `catch` or declare them — their APIs require callers to acknowledge the failure at compile time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name real checked exceptions and recognise the pattern (external/environmental failures)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing RuntimeExceptions (like NullPointerException) as checked, or not knowing InterruptedException is checked
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point out the common thread: they all represent things outside your code's control where recovery is plausible

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`IOException`, `SQLException`, `InterruptedException`, `ClassNotFoundException`, `ParseException`** are the common checked ones.
- **They extend `Exception`, not `RuntimeException`** — compiler forces `catch`/`throws`.
- **Common thread: external/environmental failures** where recovery is plausible.
- **`FileNotFoundException` is a subtype of `IOException`.**
- **`InterruptedException` requires restoring the interrupt flag** when caught.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Common checked exceptions include `IOException` for file or stream operations, `SQLException` in JDBC, `InterruptedException` from interruptible blocking methods, `ClassNotFoundException` from dynamic class loading, and `ParseException` from APIs that use that older parsing contract.

For example, `Files.readString(path)` declares `IOException`, so the caller must catch it or declare it. `Thread.sleep(...)` declares `InterruptedException`; a caller may propagate it, or if it must catch it, follow the task's interruption policy and often restore the interrupt status. These types are grouped because of Java's catch-or-declare rule. They do not all have the same cause or the same recovery action.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
`IOException` is the base for many file and stream failures, including `FileNotFoundException`. `SQLException` reports database-access failures and can carry SQL state and a vendor code. `InterruptedException` tells blocking code that another thread requested interruption; handling it is part of a cancellation policy. `ClassNotFoundException` is used when code asks for a class by name and the loader cannot find it. `ParseException` belongs to APIs such as `SimpleDateFormat` that report checked parsing failure.

The shared fact is structural: each is under `Exception` but outside `RuntimeException`, so catch-or-declare applies. Do not invent one universal response such as retrying. A missing file might use a default, a database failure might be translated, interruption may stop a task, and a bad import file may be reported to the user.

sections.title: Common Checked Exceptions
sections.content:
blue|IOException|~I/O operation failed|Files and streams|has specific subtypes|handle for this operation
emerald|SQLException|~Database access failed|SQL state and vendor code may help|translate at a data boundary|do not leak blindly
amber|InterruptedException|~Interruption request observed|sleep, wait, join, queues|propagate or follow cancellation policy|not an ordinary error
violet|Other examples|~API-specific checked types|ClassNotFoundException|ParseException|catch or declare

sections.title: Each One in Context
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling `NullPointerException`/`IllegalArgumentException` checked** — they're unchecked (`RuntimeException`).
- **Not knowing `InterruptedException` is checked** — and forgetting to restore the interrupt flag.
- **Swallowing `SQLException`** with an empty catch instead of rolling back/logging.
- **Assuming all I/O is one type** — `FileNotFoundException` is a specific `IOException` subtype.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Use the declared type to decide what this caller can actually do. Catch a checked exception here only for a real recovery, translation, or boundary response; otherwise declare it onward. For interruption, preserve the cancellation protocol rather than converting it into a generic failure without thought.

questions.question: What happens at compile time if you don't handle a checked exception?
questions.title: Compile Error for Unhandled Checked Exception
questions.direct_answer: The code **won't compile**. For a checked exception, the compiler enforces 'catch-or-declare': you must either wrap the call in a `try`/`catch` or add `throws` to the method signature. Skip both and you get a compile error like *'unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown'*. Unchecked exceptions have no such requirement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the catch-or-declare rule is enforced at compile time, not runtime
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an unhandled checked exception is a runtime error rather than a compile-time failure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the exact compiler message and contrast with unchecked, which compiles without any handling

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Unhandled checked exception = compile error**, not a runtime error.
- **Catch-or-declare**: wrap in `try`/`catch` *or* add `throws`.
- **Compiler message**: 'unreported exception … must be caught or declared'.
- **Unchecked exceptions are exempt** — no handling required to compile.
- **Don't 'fix' it with an empty catch** — handle or propagate meaningfully.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: If you don't handle a checked exception, the code simply won't compile — and that's the key point, it's a compile-time failure, not something that blows up at runtime. The compiler enforces what's called the catch-or-declare rule. Whenever you call something that can throw a checked exception, like reading a file which throws I O exception, you have two choices. Either you catch it, by wrapping the call in a try-catch block and handling it there, or you declare it, by adding throws I O exception to your method's signature so that the responsibility passes up to whoever calls your method. If you do neither, the build fails with a message along the lines of unreported exception I O exception, must be caught or declared to be thrown. So you literally can't run the program until you deal with it one way or another. That compile-time enforcement is the entire practical meaning of the word checked — the compiler won't let you silently ignore it. Compare that to unchecked exceptions, the RuntimeException subclasses: code that might throw a NullPointerException compiles perfectly fine with no handling at all, because the compiler doesn't enforce anything for those. A couple of mistakes I'd warn against: don't just slap an empty catch block on it to make the compiler happy, because that swallows real failures silently. And don't reach for throws Exception to make it go away — declare the specific exception type instead, so the contract stays honest and callers know exactly what they're dealing with.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
The compiler examines whether a checked exception can leave a method or constructor. If it can, the method must catch it or declare a compatible type in `throws`. A catch counts only when it covers the possible type, and declaring it transfers the same obligation to callers.

For example, a method calling `Files.readString(path)` does not compile until it catches `IOException` or declares it. An empty catch may satisfy the compiler but loses the failure, so compile success is not the same as correct handling. Unchecked exceptions can still be caught and documented; they simply do not take part in this compile-time rule.

sections.title: Catch-or-Declare
sections.content:
rose|Do nothing|~Compile error|'unreported exception'|build fails|never runs
blue|Catch it|~try / catch|handle here|recover or log|compiles
emerald|Declare it|~add throws|propagate to caller|caller must then handle|compiles
amber|Unchecked|~No requirement|RuntimeException|compiles with nothing|no enforcement

sections.title: Wrong: checked exception ignored -> won't compile
Right: catch it, or declare it
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting a runtime error** — it's a *compile-time* failure; the program won't build.
- **Adding an empty `catch`** just to compile — that silently swallows real failures.
- **Declaring `throws Exception`** to make it go away — declare the specific type instead.
- **Confusing it with unchecked** — `RuntimeException` code compiles with zero handling.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Catch the checked failure when this method can recover, translate it, or produce the boundary response. Otherwise declare a useful type and let a caller with more context decide. Do not add an empty catch merely to make the compiler quiet.

questions.question: Why do modern frameworks like Spring prefer unchecked exceptions?
questions.title: Why Spring Uses Unchecked Exceptions
questions.direct_answer: Spring APIs commonly use unchecked exception hierarchies so failures can cross framework callbacks and application layers without adding checked declarations to every method. Spring also translates technology-specific failures, such as `SQLException`, into its consistent unchecked `DataAccessException` hierarchy. This is an API-design choice, not proof that checked exceptions are always wrong.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the practical downsides of checked exceptions that pushed frameworks toward unchecked
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking unchecked is just 'lazier', missing that checked exceptions don't compose with lambdas/streams and leak across layers
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Spring's DataAccessException translating SQLException, and that functional interfaces can't propagate checked exceptions

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Checked exceptions add `throws`/`catch` boilerplate** at every layer.
- **They leak low-level details** (`SQLException`) into high-level code.
- **standard functional interfaces usually do not declare them** — checked breaks functional style.
- **Spring translates `SQLException` → unchecked `DataAccessException`.**
- **Result: clean signatures, decoupled layers, lambda-friendly code.**

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Spring commonly uses unchecked exception hierarchies so an application does not have to repeat checked declarations through repository, service, and controller methods that cannot handle the failure locally. It also uses exception translation: Spring data-access APIs expose the unchecked `DataAccessException` hierarchy instead of making higher layers depend directly on JDBC's `SQLException`.

For example, a service using `JdbcTemplate` can let a `DataIntegrityViolationException` reach a central handler without declaring `SQLException` in every method. Standard functional interfaces such as `Function` also do not declare arbitrary checked exceptions, although a lambda can throw a checked exception when its target interface permits it. This does not prove unchecked is always better; it shows why it fits many framework boundaries.

sections.title: Make the choice confidently
sections.content:
Unchecked exceptions reduce declaration plumbing when intermediate layers cannot recover. The stronger reason is abstraction: a service should not expose `SQLException` merely because one repository currently uses JDBC. Spring translates vendor-specific persistence failures into a stable `DataAccessException` hierarchy, whose subtypes can still distinguish constraint, connection, or query problems.

Functional APIs add another practical constraint. A lambda follows the `throws` clause of its target functional-interface method. Most standard interfaces used by streams do not declare arbitrary checked exceptions, so code must handle, adapt, or translate such a failure. Custom functional interfaces may declare one.

The trade-off is visibility. Unchecked failures do not appear in a required `throws` clause, so APIs must document important failure modes and handle them at a clear boundary.

sections.title: Why Unchecked Wins in Frameworks
sections.content:
rose|Less propagation noise|~No forced throws chain|intermediate layers can stay focused|important failures still documented|not silent handling
amber|Abstraction|~Hide vendor types|SQLException stays below data boundary|DataAccessException is stable API|preserve cause
blue|Callbacks|~Signature controls checked throws|standard Function has no throws Exception|handle or adapt inside lambda|custom interface may declare one
emerald|Trade-off|~Compiler does not force callers|central handling becomes important|choose meaningful subtypes|checked remains valid in other APIs

sections.title: Without unchecked: checked exceptions clutter every layer
sections.content:
```java
// Each layer must declare or catch the checked SQLException
User findUser(Long id) throws SQLException { return repo.find(id); }      // repo
User getUser(Long id)  throws SQLException { return findUser(id); }       // service
// And this won't even compile -- standard functional interfaces usually do not declare arbitrary checked exceptions:
ids.forEach(id -> repo.find(id));   // error: unhandled SQLException
```

sections.title: With Spring's unchecked DataAccessException
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking unchecked is just 'lazy'** — it's a deliberate API design choice for composability.
- **Forgetting standard functional interfaces usually do not declare arbitrary checked exceptions** — the real reason streams force unchecked.
- **Letting `SQLException` leak into services** instead of translating at the repository boundary.
- **Over-correcting** — genuinely recoverable, caller-actionable failures can still be checked.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: Unchecked exceptions keep framework APIs composable and avoid leaking implementation types, but the compiler does not force callers to acknowledge them. Important unchecked failures still need clear documentation, meaningful subtypes, and an application boundary that maps or logs them. Checked exceptions remain useful when a caller-facing API benefits from an explicit catch-or-declare contract.

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for Why do modern frameworks like Spring prefer unchecked exceptions? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring's DataAccessException wrapping a checked SQLException

speakable_v2.hook: Spring buries checked exceptions on purpose. One big reason, they don't even fit inside a lambda. Here's the whole story.

beats.text: Spring leans on unchecked exceptions through a trick called **exception translation**. JDBC marks SQLException as checked, while Spring's DataAccessException stays unchecked, so Spring catches one and rethrows the other. The guiding idea stays the same. checked uses catch-or-declare; unchecked does not, while recovery depends on the caller. Framework plumbing rarely needs the checked kind.

Checked exceptions have a leak problem. The moment your DAO throws SQLException, every layer above has to declare or catch that same type. Now your web layer knows about JDBC, which it has no business knowing. Translation cuts that leak.

items: **Exception translation**, catching a checked exception and rethrowing it as an unchecked one.
**DataAccessException**, Spring's unchecked family that wraps JDBC and JPA failures alike.
**The Repository annotation**, which quietly switches translation on for that bean.
Callers still catch DataAccessException when they want, since unchecked never means uncatchable.

beats.text: Here's the **non-obvious** bit. The Repository annotation isn't just a label. In a Spring context it wraps the bean in a proxy that catches vendor exceptions and turns them into DataAccessException subclasses. Lambdas push the same point. A stream's most standard functional-interface methods do not declare arbitrary checked exceptions, so an unchecked DataAccessException flows through a stream where a checked SQLException would block it.

items: Thinking DataAccessException is a checked type. It extends RuntimeException, so it's unchecked, no throws needed.
Re-catching DataAccessException in every method. Let it bubble up to a global handler.
Forgetting the Repository annotation enables translation. Miss it, and a raw NullPointerException or SQLException leaks straight through.

speakable_v2.cap: So Spring picks unchecked to keep layers clean. Translation wraps the checked stuff, so it travels up without dragging JDBC details into every signature.

questions.question: How do you wrap a checked exception in an unchecked exception?
questions.title: Wrapping Checked Exception as Unchecked in Java
questions.direct_answer: Catch the checked exception and `throw` a `RuntimeException` (or a custom unchecked subclass) that **takes the original as its cause**: `catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }`. The cause keeps the full stack trace. The JDK even provides `UncheckedIOException` for exactly this. Wrapping removes the `throws` burden from callers while preserving the root error.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can convert a checked exception to unchecked correctly, preserving the cause
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping without passing the cause, or swallowing the checked exception instead of wrapping it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention UncheckedIOException as the built-in example and that this is the standard technique for lambdas/streams

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Catch the checked exception, throw an unchecked one carrying the cause.**
- **`new RuntimeException(msg, e)`** — always pass `e` as the cause.
- **`UncheckedIOException`** is the JDK's built-in wrapper for `IOException`.
- **Useful in callbacks whose target signature does not declare the checked type**, including many standard stream operations.
- **Never swallow** the checked exception in the process.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
To translate a checked exception into an unchecked one, I catch the checked type and throw a suitable `RuntimeException` subclass with the original exception as its cause. For I/O, the JDK already provides `UncheckedIOException`.

For example: `catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException("Could not read " + path, e); }`. The outer exception gives the current operation meaning, while `getCause()` and the formatted trace retain the original I/O failure. I wrap only at a real API boundary; doing it at every method produces a noisy chain. I also do not return a made-up default unless the API explicitly defines that fallback.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Wrapping changes the exception exposed by the current API. The wrapper begins its own stack trace at the translation point, while the original remains linked through the cause. Passing only `e.getMessage()` loses that cause chain and often loses useful type-specific data.

Use a specific wrapper when possible. `UncheckedIOException` preserves an `IOException`; a repository might define an unchecked application type for a storage failure. Standard stream functional interfaces normally cannot propagate an arbitrary checked type from their method signatures, so a helper can handle or translate it before it crosses that callback boundary. This is a design decision, not permission to turn every checked exception into `RuntimeException` automatically.

sections.title: Wrapping Checked -> Unchecked
sections.content:
emerald|The pattern|~catch then throw unchecked|new RuntimeException(msg, e)|cause preserved|callers freed of throws
blue|Built-in helper|~UncheckedIOException|wraps IOException|standard JDK type|getCause() returns it
amber|Use case|~Inside standard stream callbacks|signature lacks arbitrary checked throws|wrap to propagate|functional-friendly
rose|The rule|~Always pass the cause|new X(msg) -> trace lost|new X(msg, e) -> kept|never swallow

sections.title: Wrong: swallow, or wrap without the cause
Right: wrap with the cause (or use UncheckedIOException)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrapping without the cause** — `new RuntimeException(msg)` loses the root stack trace.
- **Swallowing instead of wrapping** — returning a default hides the failure entirely.
- **Reinventing `UncheckedIOException`** — the JDK already provides it for `IOException`.
- **Wrapping everything reflexively** — only wrap when removing the checked burden genuinely helps.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Wrap when the lower-level checked type does not belong in the current API and callers should handle the failure at a different boundary. Preserve the cause and add only useful context. If the caller should make a local decision from the checked type, keep the checked contract instead.

speakable_v2.hook: You want to call a file-reading method inside a stream, but it throws a checked exception. There's a one-line idiom for that. There's also a one-word slip that ruins it.

beats.text: **Wrapping** means you catch the checked exception and rethrow it as an unchecked RuntimeException, carrying the original as the cause. That frees every caller from a throws clause. The principle underneath stays the same. checked uses catch-or-declare; unchecked does not, while recovery depends on the caller. Once recovery moves up a layer, unchecked fits.

You wrap at a layer boundary, where the lower layer's exception type has no business leaking upward. A service shouldn't throw SQLException, since that exposes the JDBC guts underneath. So it throws its own DataException instead, in its own vocabulary.

items: Catch the checked exception inside a try-catch.
Throw a new unchecked exception, passing the original in as the cause.
Always chain the cause, like new DataException with the message and the original error.
Prefer a named exception over a bare RuntimeException, so callers can catch it precisely.

beats.text: Here's the **non-obvious** part. The JDK already ships UncheckedIOException for exactly this, wrapping a checked IOException as an unchecked one. So inside a stream, where the functional interfaces refuse checked exceptions, you catch the IOException from Files readString and rethrow it as UncheckedIOException. The exception rides cleanly out, and the cause still points at the real failure.

items: Wrapping without the cause. The original stack trace vanishes, and production logs go blind.
Throwing a plain RuntimeException instead of a named one. Callers can't single it out.
Wrapping in every method. Only wrap when you actually cross a boundary.

speakable_v2.cap: So wrap at the boundary, always chain the cause, and reach for a named exception. UncheckedIOException is the JDK's own take on the pattern.

questions.question: Why is InterruptedException a checked exception?
questions.title: Why InterruptedException is Checked
questions.direct_answer: `InterruptedException` is checked so code calling interruptible blocking methods must decide what interruption means for that operation. If a method can propagate it, let it propagate. If code catches it but cannot rethrow it, it normally restores the interrupt status and stops or returns according to its cancellation policy. Interruption is a request, not a forced command to terminate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand interruption as a cooperative cancellation signal and the correct handling pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Swallowing InterruptedException with an empty catch, destroying the interrupt status
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that catching it clears the interrupt flag, so you must restore it (or rethrow) so callers can also react

sections.title: Interruption Is a Request, Not a Kill
sections.content:
**`InterruptedException`** is thrown by blocking calls — `Thread.sleep()`, `Object.wait()`, `Thread.join()`, blocking queue operations — when another thread **interrupts** the blocked one. Interruption in Java is **cooperative**: it's a polite *request* to stop, not a forced kill. The thread gets to decide how to respond.

It's **checked** precisely to force that decision — the compiler makes you write a handler rather than ignore a cancellation signal. The catch is subtle: when the exception is thrown, the JVM **clears** the thread's interrupt flag. So the correct handling is to **restore it** with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` (or rethrow `InterruptedException`) so code higher up can also notice the interruption and shut down cleanly.

sections.title: Handling InterruptedException
sections.content:
blue|Cooperative signal|~Request, not forced kill|blocking method observes interrupt|operation stops waiting|task chooses response
amber|Checked contract|~Caller must decide|propagate when signature allows|otherwise handle deliberately|do not swallow
emerald|Status rule|~Throwing usually clears status|restore when code must preserve request|then return or stop by policy|avoid blind retry
violet|Boundary|~Cancellation belongs to owner|library code should not invent shutdown|cleanup still applies|document behavior

sections.title: Wrong: swallowing it destroys the interrupt signal
Right: restore the flag and stop gracefully
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Empty catch:** loses the interruption request and can make shutdown hang.
- **Always restoring and continuing:** restoring is useful only with a policy that will observe it; do not keep retrying the same blocking call forever.
- **Treating `interrupt()` as a kill:** it sets a status and causes certain blocking operations to react; the task still cooperates.
- **Converting it to a generic exception without the cause:** this hides the cancellation signal and diagnostic trail.
- **Assuming one response fits every API:** propagate when possible; otherwise follow the owner-defined cancellation policy.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Interruption is cooperative** — a request to stop, not a forced kill.
- **It's checked to force a conscious decision** on cancellation.
- **Catching `InterruptedException` clears the interrupt flag.**
- **Restore it** with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` or rethrow.
- **Never swallow it** with an empty catch — the thread becomes uncancellable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`InterruptedException` is checked, so a caller of an interruptible blocking method must make an explicit decision about the interruption. Methods such as `sleep`, `wait`, `join`, and blocking-queue operations can throw it when interruption is observed.

Interruption is a cooperative request, not a forced thread stop. For example, a worker whose method already declares `throws InterruptedException` can let it propagate to its task boundary. If a method cannot propagate it, a common policy is to call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` to restore the status and then return or stop its loop. The exact action belongs to the task's cancellation contract; blindly swallowing it makes cancellation unreliable.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Thread.sleep in a loop, re-interrupting on catch
familiarity_anchors: swallowing InterruptedException with an empty catch
speakable_v2.hook: Catch InterruptedException with an empty block and you've quietly made your thread impossible to cancel. One line, and the whole shutdown jams.

beats.text: Java makes **InterruptedException** checked because an interrupt is a planned signal, not a bug. When one thread interrupts another, the JVM clears the interrupt flag and throws it out of sleep or wait. The compiler then makes the blocked thread react.

Interruption is how one thread asks another to stop. An executor winding down sends interrupts to its workers. If a thread swallows the signal in silence, it ignores the request and just keeps running. So the compiler won't let that signal slip away.

items: **Option one, re-interrupt:** call Thread currentThread interrupt to restore the flag so callers still see it.
**Option two, propagate:** declare throws InterruptedException and let the caller decide.
**Option three, last resort:** wrap it as a RuntimeException, only when propagating truly isn't possible.

beats.text: Here's the **non-obvious** trap. Catching the exception clears the interrupt flag as a side effect. So an empty catch wipes the signal, and code upstream that checks isInterrupted thinks all is well. Now nothing can cancel the thread. The fix is small, restore the flag with Thread currentThread interrupt, then break out and let the thread wind down.

items: An empty catch on InterruptedException. It silently breaks cancellation in thread pools.
Forgetting to re-interrupt after the catch. The catch already cleared the flag for you.
Wrapping it as a RuntimeException without re-interrupting. Upstream callers then miss the interrupt.

speakable_v2.cap: So Java marks it checked because ignoring it silently breaks clean thread cancellation. Always re-interrupt or propagate, never just swallow it.
